questions.title: Regular expressions
questions.question: Which object is a regular expression rather than a language or a machine?

options.label: The set of all words ending in ab

questions.explanation: An expression is syntax that describes a set. The set is its language; the five-tuple specifies an automaton.

questions.title: Regular expressions
questions.question: Over {a,b,c}, what language does a|bc describe?
questions.explanation: Concatenation binds before alternation: the choices are a and the two-symbol word bc. Parentheses would be needed for (a|b)c.

questions.title: Regular expressions
questions.question: Which word matches a(b|c)d?
questions.explanation: Choose c from the alternation, then concatenate a, c, d. The choice contributes exactly one of b or c.

questions.title: Regular expressions
questions.question: Which expression describes exactly {ε,a}?
questions.explanation: a* also contains aa; ∅|a and εa both describe only {a}. Alternation with ε explicitly adds the empty word.

questions.title: Regular expressions
questions.question: Which expression describes binary words containing 01 somewhere?
questions.explanation: Arbitrary binary prefixes and suffixes surround 01. The other expressions impose a prefix, a suffix, or repetitions of the entire block.

questions.title: Regular expressions
questions.question: Which word matches ab* but does not match (ab)*?
questions.explanation: ab* contains one a followed by any number of b symbols, so abb belongs. (ab)* repeats the whole block; ab belongs to both, abab only to the latter, and ε only to the latter.

questions.title: Regular expressions
questions.question: Which pair describes the same language?
questions.explanation: Repeated alternatives do not duplicate words in a set. a* includes ε whereas aa* does not; the other pairs differ in order or length.

questions.title: Regular expressions
questions.question: Which expression denotes no words at all?
questions.explanation: Concatenating with the empty language gives the empty language. aεb denotes ab; ∅* and ε each denote {ε}.

questions.title: Regular expressions
questions.question: Which statement follows from a regex specification of an identifier?

options.label: A parser is unnecessary for an entire programming language.
The identifier's variable type is determined by the regex.
A scanner can use it to recognize identifier lexemes.
Every sequence of valid tokens is a valid program.

questions.explanation: Regexes can specify lexical patterns. Grammar, type checks, and program meaning require additional processing.

questions.title: Regular expressions
questions.question: Consider formal regexes without star, built from finitely many symbols, ε, ∅, union and concatenation. Which is guaranteed?

options.label: Their languages contain exactly one word.

questions.explanation: Finite unions and concatenations of finite languages stay finite. This does not imply that any expression containing star has an infinite language: ε* is a counterexample.

questions.title: Concatenation
questions.question: If x=01 and y=10, what is xy?
questions.explanation: Concatenate the two sequences without deleting or reordering symbols. A set containing x and y is not their concatenation.

questions.title: Concatenation
questions.question: Let R={a,b} and S={0,1}. What is RS?
questions.explanation: Every left word combines with every right word, giving all four pairs in that order.

questions.title: Concatenation
questions.question: For any language L, what is L{ε}?
questions.explanation: Appending the empty word changes no word. It does not add ε unless ε already belongs to L.

questions.title: Concatenation
questions.question: For any language L, what is L∅?
questions.explanation: There is no right-hand word available, so no concatenation can be formed. This differs from concatenation with {ε}.

questions.title: Concatenation
questions.question: Which identity holds for all languages R,S,T?
questions.explanation: Concatenation is associative and distributes over union, not intersection in this form. Order generally matters.

questions.title: Concatenation
questions.question: Let R={ε,a}, S={ε,a}. How many distinct words are in RS?
questions.explanation: RS={ε,a,aa}. Two different pairs produce a, so multiplying cardinalities can overcount distinct concatenated words.

questions.title: Concatenation
questions.question: For which condition is ε in RS?

options.label: R and S share any word.
R and S are both nonempty.
ε is in both R and S.
ε is in at least one of R and S.

questions.explanation: Word lengths add. To obtain length zero, both component words must have length zero.

questions.title: Concatenation
questions.question: Which word proves ab* is not the same as a*b?
questions.explanation: a is in ab* by taking zero b symbols, but is not in a*b, which requires a final b. The other listed words do not distinguish the pair.

questions.title: Concatenation
questions.question: If RS=∅, what must hold?

options.label: At least one of R or S is empty.
Both R and S are empty.

questions.explanation: If both sets had a word, concatenating those words would produce an element of RS. Disjointness is irrelevant.

questions.title: Concatenation
questions.question: Let R={ε,a} and S={b}. Which equality is correct?
questions.explanation: Choose ε or a from R, then append b. The two products are εb=b and ab.

questions.title: Alternation
questions.question: What does R|S mean for the described languages?
questions.explanation: Alternation admits a word if either branch admits it. It does not require both branches or concatenate their words.

questions.title: Alternation
questions.question: What does 10|01 match?
questions.explanation: The two alternatives are whole words of length two. No surrounding star allows extra input.

questions.title: Alternation
questions.question: If a word satisfies both branches of R|S, what happens?

options.label: It appears twice as distinct set elements.
It belongs to the language once.

questions.explanation: Union is inclusive and languages are sets; multiple descriptions of a word do not create duplicate elements.

questions.title: Alternation
questions.question: Which expression equals (a|b)c?
questions.explanation: Concatenation distributes across alternation. Each alternative must receive the trailing c.

questions.title: Alternation
questions.question: Which equality holds for every language R?
questions.explanation: The empty language contributes no words. Adding {ε} may add a new word, and duplicate union is R rather than R*.

questions.title: Alternation
questions.question: For R={a,ab} and S={ab,b}, how many words are in R∪S?
questions.explanation: The union is {a,ab,b}; the shared word ab is counted once.

questions.title: Alternation
questions.question: Over binary words, L means 'odd number of 0s OR even number of 1s'. Does 011 belong?

options.label: Yes; only the first condition holds.

questions.explanation: 011 has one 0 and two 1s. Inclusive OR accepts when both conditions hold as well as when exactly one holds.

questions.title: Alternation
questions.question: If R∪S is regular, what can be concluded about R and S individually?
questions.explanation: Let R be nonregular and S its complement: the union is Σ*, which is regular. Conversely, regular components can also have a regular union.

questions.title: Alternation
questions.question: Which word distinguishes a*|b* from (a|b)*?
questions.explanation: (a|b)* allows mixing letters in one word. a*|b* allows only all-a or all-b words, including ε.

questions.title: Alternation
questions.question: If ε is not in R but is in S, is ε in R∪S?

options.label: Yes, because membership in one branch is enough.
No, because both branches must contain it.

questions.explanation: Union needs one membership witness. The size of S and whether R is empty do not change this.

questions.title: Repetition and Kleene star
questions.question: Which word belongs to R* for every language R?
questions.explanation: Zero repetitions are always allowed, even if R is empty.

questions.title: Repetition and Kleene star
questions.question: What is ∅*?
questions.explanation: Zero factors produce ε, and positive numbers of factors are impossible because ∅ has no words. ∅ is a set, not an input word.

questions.title: Repetition and Kleene star
questions.question: What is {ε}*?
questions.explanation: Concatenating any number of empty words still yields the same empty word.

questions.title: Repetition and Kleene star
questions.question: Which word belongs to (ab|ba)*?
questions.explanation: abba splits as ab followed by ba. Every permitted block has length two and is ab or ba.

questions.title: Repetition and Kleene star
questions.question: Which description is exact for (aa)*?

options.label: All even-length words over {a}, including ε

questions.explanation: Every repetition contributes two a symbols; zero repetitions contribute length zero.

questions.title: Repetition and Kleene star
questions.question: For L=(110*)*, which statement is true?

options.label: Every maximal run of 1s has even length.
Every word has even total length.
No word contains 111 as a substring.

questions.explanation: Each block contributes 11 and any number of 0s. Adjacent blocks may merge runs of 1s, preserving even run length. 110 has odd length; 1111 contains 111; 11 needs no 0.

questions.title: Repetition and Kleene star
questions.question: Which pair is equivalent?
questions.explanation: A sequence of sequences of a symbols is still any finite sequence of a symbols. The other pairs differ on mixed, repeated, or empty words.

questions.title: Repetition and Kleene star
questions.question: When is L* finite?

options.label: Exactly when L is a subset of {ε}.

questions.explanation: Any nonempty-length word w in L gives distinct w^k of unbounded length. If L contains only ε, or is empty, L*={ε}.

questions.title: Repetition and Kleene star
questions.question: Let P={a^p : p is prime}. What is P*?
questions.explanation: Lengths 2 and 3 are prime. Every even n≥2 uses 2s; every odd n≥3 uses one 3 and 2s. Length 1 is impossible, and ε uses zero blocks.

questions.title: Repetition and Kleene star
questions.question: Which expression describes one or more repetitions of R?
questions.explanation: RR* requires at least one factor from R. If ε belongs to L(R), one or more factors may still yield the empty word; 'one factor' need not mean 'one symbol'.

questions.title: Language
questions.question: Which statement defines a language over Σ?
questions.explanation: A language is a set of finite words whose symbols come from Σ. It need not include every possible word.

questions.title: Language
questions.question: How many words are in {ε}?
questions.explanation: The set has one element, the empty word. Its word has length zero, but its cardinality is one.

questions.title: Language
questions.question: How many words are in ∅?
questions.explanation: The empty language has no elements, including no empty word.

questions.title: Language
questions.question: Let L={0,01}. Which statement is correctly typed and true?
questions.explanation: 01 is a word and is an element of L. The singleton language {01} is a subset of L, not one of its word elements.

questions.title: Language
questions.question: Can an infinite language contain only finite words?

options.label: No; some word must be infinite.
Only if its alphabet is infinite.

questions.explanation: Infinite describes the number of words, not the length of an individual word. a* has infinitely many finite words over one symbol and is regular.

questions.title: Language
questions.question: For a finite nonempty alphabet, which statement is true?

options.label: There is a longest word in Σ*.
There are finitely many words of any fixed length.
Every language over it is finite.

questions.explanation: At length n there are |Σ|^n words. Allowing all finite lengths gives unbounded word length and infinitely many words.

questions.title: Language
questions.question: Let Σ={0,1} and L={0,1}. What is Σ*\L?

options.label: Only words of length at least two
All binary words except the two one-symbol words

questions.explanation: The complement includes ε and all words of length at least two, while excluding exactly 0 and 1.

questions.title: Language
questions.question: If L={ab,ab,ε}, how many distinct words does L contain?
questions.explanation: Sets ignore duplicates. The two distinct elements are ab and ε.

questions.title: Language
questions.question: Over a finite alphabet, every infinite language has which property?
questions.explanation: Bounded lengths permit only finitely many words. Infinite languages may omit many lengths, omit ε, and be regular or nonregular.

questions.title: Language
questions.question: Which statement separates a language from a regular expression?

options.label: Every regex describes exactly one word.
Every language has a regular expression.
Every language is itself a regex string.
Different expressions can describe the same set of words.

questions.explanation: Languages are semantic sets; regexes are descriptions of regular languages. For instance, a|a and a describe the same singleton set.

questions.title: Alphabet
questions.question: If Σ={a,b}, which is an alphabet symbol?
questions.explanation: a is an atomic symbol in Σ; ab is a two-symbol word, ε is the empty word, and {a} is a set.

questions.title: Alphabet
questions.question: For Σ={0,1}, what is Σ^0?
questions.explanation: There is exactly one sequence of zero symbols: ε. The numeral 0 is a one-symbol word, not the empty word.

questions.title: Alphabet
questions.question: For Σ={x,y}, what is Σ^2?
questions.explanation: Choose either symbol independently at each of two positions; order matters.

questions.title: Alphabet
questions.question: If |Σ|=3, how many words have length four?
questions.explanation: Each position has three choices, giving 3^4=81. Multiplying length by alphabet size counts the wrong object.

questions.title: Alphabet
questions.question: Is ε in Σ* for Σ={a}?

options.label: No, because ε is not an alphabet symbol.
Yes, because length zero is allowed.
Only if ε is added to Σ.
Only if a is removed from Σ.

questions.explanation: Σ* contains sequences of every finite length, including zero. ε need not be a symbol to be a word.

questions.title: Alphabet
questions.question: For Σ={0,1}, which word is outside Σ*?
questions.explanation: 102 uses 2, which is not in the alphabet. Repetition of allowed symbols and the empty word are permitted.

questions.title: Alphabet
questions.question: With token kinds treated as atomic symbols, Σ={ID,NUM,PLUS}. What is the length of the sequence ID NUM PLUS?
questions.explanation: Length counts the declared atomic symbols, not the printed letters in their names.

questions.title: Alphabet
questions.question: If Σ={a} and Γ={a,b}, which relation is true?

options.label: Σ* is a proper subset of Γ*.
Γ* is a proper subset of Σ*.

questions.explanation: Every a-word is a Γ-word, but b is a Γ-word that is not a Σ-word. Both sets contain ε.

questions.title: Alphabet
questions.question: What does Σ^3 mean?

options.label: All words of length at most three
Three copies of Σ as one alphabet symbol
All words with three distinct symbols
All words of exactly three symbols

questions.explanation: Positions may repeat a symbol. The exponent here specifies exact length, not an upper bound or a distinctness condition.

questions.title: Alphabet
questions.question: For Σ={a,b}, how many words have length at most two?
questions.explanation: Count length zero, one and two: 1+2+4=7. Omitting ε gives the tempting wrong answer 6.

questions.title: String or word
questions.question: What is |ε|?
questions.explanation: The empty word has zero symbols; it is still a word.

questions.title: String or word
questions.question: For w=00101, what is |w|0?
questions.explanation: There are three zero positions. The two ones contribute to total length but not to |w|0.

questions.title: String or word
questions.question: For w=ab, what is w^3?
questions.explanation: Exponentiation of a word means concatenating three copies of the whole word.

questions.title: String or word
questions.question: Which statement about w=010 is true?
questions.explanation: The two zeros are separated. Prefix, suffix, count and adjacency are different properties.

questions.title: String or word
questions.question: Under the usual nonempty-word interpretation, does the word 1 begin and end with the same symbol?

options.label: Only if the alphabet is unary.
Yes; its first and last position are the same position.
Only if ε also belongs to the language.

questions.explanation: A one-symbol word has both a first and a last symbol. A length-at-least-two restriction must be stated separately.

questions.title: String or word
questions.question: Which statement about 1111 is true?

options.label: It has a maximal run of exactly three 1s.
It contains 111 but has no maximal run of exactly three 1s.
It contains exactly three 1s in total.

questions.explanation: There are length-three substrings at positions 1-3 and 2-4, but the whole maximal run has length four.

questions.title: String or word
questions.question: If |x|=2 and |y|=5, what is |xy|?
questions.explanation: Concatenation keeps all positions, so lengths add. Matching symbols at a boundary are not merged.

questions.title: String or word
questions.question: What is the reverse of 00101?
questions.explanation: Reversal changes position order; it does not complement the bits.

questions.title: String or word
questions.question: Which description of ε is correct?

options.label: It can only be concatenated with itself.
It is a prefix and a suffix of every word.
It is the same object as ∅.
It is a one-symbol substring of every word.

questions.explanation: For every word w, εw=w=wε. It has no symbol and is distinct from the empty set.

questions.title: String or word
questions.question: Over {0,1}, compare 'length is even' and 'number of 1s is even'. Which is true?

options.label: Even length implies an even number of 1s.
An even number of 1s implies even length.

questions.explanation: 01 has even length but one 1; 0 has odd length but zero 1s. Zero is even.

questions.title: Regular language
questions.question: Which is a base case in the recursive definition of regular languages?

options.label: Every language with equal numbers of two symbols

questions.explanation: {ε}, ∅, and {a} for a∈Σ are the base cases. Arbitrary subsets need not be regular.

questions.title: Regular language
questions.question: Is every finite language regular?

options.label: No; only singleton languages are regular.
No; ε makes a finite language nonregular.
Yes; use a finite union of expressions for its words.

questions.explanation: Each finite word is a finite concatenation of symbols. Finite union handles all words, with ∅ for the empty language.

questions.title: Regular language
questions.question: Which language is infinite and regular?
questions.explanation: The first is described by a*. The other three are nonregular examples established in this module.

questions.title: Regular language
questions.question: Which operation is part of the recursive construction of regular languages?
questions.explanation: Star is a defining regular operation. Finite union is allowed; arbitrary infinite union need not preserve regularity.

questions.title: Regular language
questions.question: Which statement follows if a DFA recognizes L?

options.label: L has a unique regular expression.

questions.explanation: DFA-recognizable languages are regular. DFAs can recognize infinite languages and can reject ε; descriptions need not be unique.
